verdicts.note: Methodological survey of Japanese historical demography sources.
Ex-nuptiality and cohabitation in New Zealand; no parental co-residence.
Co-residence with the husband's parents at the start of marriage, and its duration, against reproduction in Taiwan 1973-80. Directly on cell.
Plasmid-coded endonuclease in bacteria.
Comment on household formation as the route from economic change to English fertility, 18th-19th century. Pre-modern niche; A.7's under Ruling 2.
Loss of control in women alcoholics; children living at home is a covariate.
Czechoslovak youth policy profile; housing support is described, not estimated.
Czechoslovak census household types 1970-80 with fertility by social class described alongside; no arrangement-to-fertility estimate.
Structural model of childbearing and abortion attitudes in Japan; no arrangement exposure.
Child support law; 'children living with one parent' is post-divorce custody.
Genetic counselling and pregnancy intentions.

Household type against family size, Maharashtra 1970, finding HIGHER fertility in nuclear than extended households and ruling out several explanations. Sign runs against the extended-household prediction.
Household organisation by class among Languedoc winegrowers; inheritance and fertility shape household form, so the arrow runs toward the arrangement.
Adult attitudes to family-planning education.
Staff nurse job satisfaction; children living at home is a covariate.
France country profile, census description.
Formal fertility models with unequal bequest and primogeniture in pre-industrial England; inheritance rules set who stays. Theory, pre-modern.
Anthropological definition of the household as a unit; conceptual, useful for the measurement question in §9.
Characteristics of families with Down's syndrome children; 'living at home' describes the index child.

Runs the arrow the chapter's way round backwards and is valuable for it: marriage, military service, employment and PARENTHOOD are the predictors and residential dependence on parents is the outcome. Direct documentation of threat 2, reverse causation.
Age at leaving the parental home among 19th-century New England manufacturers; economic determinants, no fertility outcome, pre-modern.
Education and fertility in Japan; no arrangement exposure.
Nurses' work self-disclosure, burnout and marital satisfaction.

Social policy effects on marriage, fertility and household formation in Britain. Policy is the exposure and household formation one outcome among several; possible design-6 lead, worth a full-text look.
Canadian income inequality; fertility appears as a background trend.
Family variables and child weight change; 'persons living at home' is a covariate.

Distinguishes multigenerational households located in the PARENT's home from those in the CHILD's home, and says the distinction carries the dependency direction. That is §6's wall stated by the field itself; read in full when the wall is written up.
Simulation in which declining FERTILITY changes Chinese family size and structure. The arrow runs from fertility to the arrangement.
Formal household-cycle demography; fission, fusion and household size.
Shiftwork and role strain in dual-earner couples.
Arranged versus free-market marriage and fertility in Japan; C.7.a's matching question, not the arrangement.
Managing personal transitions; 'children leaving home' is one item in a list of life events.
Chinese family-planning outreach practice.

Waite and Goldscheider on nonfamily living: time spent living away from the parental home before marriage against later family orientations, NLS young men and women. A pre-launch record with the arrow the right way round, and the predicted sign is the OPPOSITE of A.23's -- independent living is argued to ERODE family orientation. Priority read.
Framework essay on age-sex roles and demographic change.
Household formation in developed societies as a demand-supply problem, with nine hypotheses for the trend toward separate living. The theory statement for link 1.
Hajnal's household formation rules extended to stem-family Japan, relating household formation to fertility. Pre-modern; A.7's under Ruling 2 but directly relevant framing.
Work-nonwork conflict among MBAs; children living at home is a covariate.

Household type against fertility preferences and current fertility, national probability sample of Taiwanese women, with marital duration controlled. Finds only a slight extended-household difference once duration is held fixed.
Book review, no abstract, title not decisive.
Yoruba working mothers and childcare; kin support is described but the exposure is employment.

Korean couples living with parents-in-law versus independently, compared on MARITAL ADJUSTMENT. The arrangement is the exposure and the comparison is exactly the chapter's, but the outcome is not fertility.
Women's status and fertility in Thailand; intra-familial decision making is the exposure, not co-residence.
Journal version of the New England age-at-leaving-home study; economic determinants, no fertility outcome.
Living arrangements and familial contacts of the ELDERLY in Japan; the homonym.
Child-shifting and fosterage in Antigua as a household strategy; children move, not young adults.
Determinants of the Egyptian fertility transition; no arrangement exposure.
No abstract; the title -- recent trends in family and household composition in Europe -- places it in the exposure-trend stream but nothing more is visible.
Procedural history of the NSFH survey design.
Dutch households' response to falling real income.
Lesthaeghe's ideational-change model of Western family formation. D.1.a's.
Survey of urban Chinese family structure, nuclear versus stem shares; descriptive, establishes the exposure trend in a setting the chapter needs.
Migration, marriage process and household formation among Bolivian peasants, with the onset of childbearing in scope. Worth a full-text read for whether an arrangement-to-birth estimate exists.
Stem-family functioning in the Pyrenees before 1914, with marital fertility limitation as a Malthusian check. Pre-modern; A.7's under Ruling 2.
Women's work and family obligation in 19th-century Verviers; book review.
